prime.problem: With 3 characters of context the model almost never sees a whole name, so it guesses where a name ends from its last few letters. Before building a new architecture you need to know how far just showing it more characters gets you, or you can't tell whether the fancy version actually helped.
prime.fits: It reuses the flat MLP you packaged with Embedding, Flatten and Sequential, and the rolling-window dataset from the MLP lecture. It sets the number (val 2.0342 at 22,097 parameters) that the WaveNet-style tree on the next cards has to beat.
prime.goal: Predict how the dataset, the parameter count and the loss change when you widen the context, and explain why a flat layer is a weak way to use that context.

attend: Which tensor gets wider when block_size goes from 3 to 8, and which one stays exactly the same size?
Which single weight matrix absorbs all 10,000 new parameters, and why does no other layer notice the change?
Why does seeing the whole name matter most for the row whose target is the final '.'?
The val loss improves but the train–val gap more than doubles. What does that say about how the flat layer uses the extra context?
Why does this baseline have to be kept at about 22K parameters before the tree model can be judged against it?

must: build_dataset emits one row per character to predict → block_size only sets each row's width → 182,625 rows either way, now of shape (182625, 8) → more information per example, not more examples
Embedding is per character and output is per prediction → only the first Linear sees n_embd·block_size inputs → its weights go 30×200 → 80×200 → all +10,000 params land there (12,097 → 22,097)
Wider window → 94.7% of training names fit whole (vs 2.0%) → the model sees more of the name before predicting → val 2.1065 → 2.0342

One Linear mixes all 80 numbers in a single matmul → every character pair must be combined at once → context is squashed early, and the train–val gap grows 0.048 → 0.118 → motivates fusing characters gradually in a tree
elevated: Most rows are mostly padding (96.8% of block_size-8 rows contain at least one '.' pad) → the first layer spends weights on positions that are usually '.' → widening further (e.g. 16) buys mostly padding
reference: the notebook's commented n_hidden = 300 (32,997 params) vs the 200 that gives 22,097
the step-0 loss 3.2847 and the lab's --quick result (train 2.0770 / val 2.1074)

compress.prompt: From memory, explain in 3–5 sentences what changes when block_size goes from 3 to 8: in the dataset, in the model, and in the loss. Or draw the flat model on one row and mark the one layer that grows.
checklist: same number of rows (182,625), each now 8 indices wide
only the first Linear grows: 80×200 instead of 30×200, +10,000 params, 22,097 total
most names now fit whole in the window, so val drops from about 2.11 to about 2.03
the train–val gap grows, a sign the flat layer overfits more
the limit: one layer squashes all 8 characters at once, which the tree model addresses

retrieve.q: Explain why going from 3 to 8 characters of context helps a character-level name model, using the fraction of names that fit in the window.
answer: at 3, only 2.0% of training names fit whole; at 8, 94.7% do
the model sees more of the name, especially when predicting the end '.'

retrieve.q: Walk one batch of 32 rows through the block_size-8 flat model and give the tensor shape after each layer.
Compute the parameter count for block_size 8 with n_embd 10 and n_hidden 200, and say which term would change if you went to block_size 16.
answer: only the first Linear's (n_embd·block_size)·n_hidden term changes: 160×200 = 32,000, total 38,097

retrieve.q: Your colleague wants to fix the model by widening the window to 16. What does it cost, what might it buy, and what doesn't it fix?
answer: buys little: the longest name has 15 letters, so rows are mostly padding
doesn't fix the core limit: one layer still squashes all characters at once
and it isn't measured here: you'd have to run it

compare.q: The flat block_size-8 MLP vs the 3-level hierarchical net at about the same 22K parameters: what is fundamentally different about how each combines the 8 characters, and why did the first hierarchical run still only tie?
answer: flat: one Linear on all 80 numbers at once; tree: pairs, then pairs of pairs, then the final pair (3 levels of 2-way fusion)
the first tree run scored val 2.029 vs 2.027 (notebook): a BatchNorm bug and no tuning
pick flat for a quick baseline, the tree when you want to spend parameters on gradual fusion

compare.q: The MLP lecture built rows with a 3-character window; this card uses the same code with 8. What is identical, what changes, and what would break if you changed block_size but forgot to rebuild the model?
answer: identical: the sliding crop-and-append loop and the number of rows
changes: each row's width, and the first Linear's fan-in (n_embd·block_size)
forgetting to rebuild: Flatten gives (B, 80) but the Linear expects 30 inputs, so the matmul raises a shape error

predict.q: Suppose names.txt had names up to 30 letters long, but the average stayed about 6. Would widening from 8 to 32 help the flat model much? Commit to a guess and a reason.
predict.answer: Probably only a little, and it could hurt. The first Linear would grow to 320×200 = 64,000 weights, but for most rows the extra 24 positions are just '.' padding. The few long names would gain context; everything else pays the parameter cost and the extra room to overfit. This is illustrative reasoning, not a measured result: the fix the lecture takes is to change how the context is combined (a tree), not only how much of it there is.

apply.task: Run labs/more-context-baseline.py --quick (20,000 steps), then change block_size to 3 in a copy and run it again. Compare the parameter counts and the val losses, and check your prediction of the row count before looking.
apply.done: The block_size-8 quick run prints 22,097 parameters and val 2.1074; your block_size-3 copy prints 12,097 parameters and the same 182,625 rows, and you can say which val is lower.
apply.hint: Only the block_size = 8 line needs to change; flat_model and splits take it as an argument. The full 200k-step runs give val 2.1065 (3) and 2.0342 (8).

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: the row count, or the parameter count?
What couldn't you explain cleanly about why only one layer grows?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: wider window → more of the name visible, or wider single layer → bigger train–val gap?
Could you argue, with numbers, why widening to 16 isn't the next step?
What will you look for when the tree model is compared against 2.0342 on the next cards?
